content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guideline for the screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer. This is the second edition of the guideline and includes recommendations for the use of messenger RNA (mRNA) tests for detecting human papillomavirus (HPV). The guideline is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-004043-4 and 978-92-4-004044-1. The guideline includes acknowledgments for contributions from various groups and individuals, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the External Review Group (ERG), and other external contributors. Special thanks are extended to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) for their literature reviews, which were instrumental in the guideline development process. The systematic review process was led by Nancy Santesso from McMaster University, with contributions from systematic review teams. The guideline development process was supported by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) Secretariat and the WHO Steering Group. The GDG included experts from diverse fields, and their names are listed in the annexes of the publication. Observers at the GDG meetings and members of the WHO Secretariat also contributed to the process. Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of mortality among women, with an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths worldwide in 2020. It is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 23 countries and the leading cause of cancer death in 36 countries, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa, Melanesia, South America, and South-Eastern Asia. In May 2018, WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for the elimination of cervical cancer. In November 2020, the Global Strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer was launched, with targets for 2030 including 90% HPV vaccination coverage for eligible girls, 70% screening coverage with a high-performance test, and 90% appropriate management of women with positive screening tests or cervical lesions. Following the launch of the Global Strategy, experts identified key areas to increase access to screening and treatment to meet the 2030 targets. One focus area was updating WHO recommendations for cervical cancer prevention, including simplifying screening and treatment algorithms. The updated guideline and recommendations are being developed in four phases. This current guideline delivers recommendations for the use of HPV mRNA tests for screening to detect cervical pre-cancer and prevent cervical cancer. Two approaches to screening and treatment are outlined in the guideline: 1. The screen-and-treat approach, where treatment decisions are based solely on a positive primary screening test. 2. The screen, triage, and treat approach, where treatment decisions are based on a positive primary screening test followed by a positive secondary (triage) test, with or without histological confirmation. HPV E6/E7 mRNA detection is presented as an alternative to HPV DNA tests for HPV detection. mRNA technologies detect the mRNA of E6/E7 oncoproteins, which are responsible for HPV-mediated oncogenic transformation of epithelial cells. This method may be more specific than HPV DNA detection, as mRNA tests correlate with active virus replication, which is further along the pathway toward pre-cancer development. Most HPV DNA tests target 13–14 oncogenic HPV types, while mRNA tests vary, with some targeting all 14 oncogenic types and others targeting fewer. The guideline was developed following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014). The GDG, formed in early 2019, identified 13 clinical algorithms for screening and treatment, prioritizing seven for evaluation in the first iteration of the updated guideline. Four additional algorithms are addressed in this publication. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were conducted to evaluate the accuracy of HPV mRNA testing in screening and treatment algorithms. Modeling studies assessed the impact and cost-effectiveness of different strategies. Existing reports on acceptability, feasibility, resources, and equity aspects of HPV testing were also utilized. This publication focuses on recommendations for the use of HPV mRNA testing to prevent cervical cancer.
